Adel is also the co-founder of InspiredK.org, a certified 501(c)(3) nonprofit dedicated to empowering highschool students, college learners, and young adults through hands-on learning in Artificial Intelligence, science, and engineering research.
summary:
NISAR, the NASA-ISRO Synthetic Aperture Radar, is the first satellite to carry two radars: NASA’s L-band and ISRO’s S-band. Their public archives already hold about 7.58 petabytes, far more raw radar data than most people can ever use. We developed Project Zeta, a website that turns petabytes of raw radar data into answers anyone can access.

Project Zeta addresses the challenge by using both of NISAR’s radars to show how Earth’s surface changes and to explain why. It covers 206 sites around the world, including 6 around our very own Space City, across 12 kinds of change, from wildfires and floods to glaciers and earthquakes. Radar statistics measure each change, six machine learning models name the changes, and every published site passed a test against independent data under a rule written down before scoring. Visitors can follow a guided story for each site, sweep between two dates or two radars, and look up what NISAR sees at any point on Earth.

Project Zeta is important because radar works through cloud, smoke, and darkness, yet its data rarely reaches the people who need it. Our maps can serve fire agencies, flood responders, farmers, city planners, and students alike. Making all of NISAR’s raw archive public in one place on cloud storage would cost over $100,000 a month; Project Zeta’s approach could cover all of NISAR’s land, visualize it, and interpret it for about $150 a month. It turns a new mission’s first data into trusted answers for everyone.
details:
Overview

NISAR, the NASA-ISRO Synthetic Aperture Radar, is the first satellite to carry two radars: NASA’s L-band (about 24 cm wavelength) and ISRO’s S-band (about 9.4 cm wavelength). Together, their public archives already hold about 7.58 petabytes in more than 1.2 million files, growing by about 43 TB a day. Very few people can use that much raw radar data. Project Zeta turns those petabytes of raw radar data into maps and answers anyone can read in their web browser.

Project Zeta reads NISAR data for 206 sites around the world, including 6 around our very own Space City. The sites cover 12 kinds of processes: wildfires, deforestation, floods and wetlands, agriculture, soil moisture, glaciers, sea ice, subsidence, earthquakes, volcanoes, built-up land, and forest biomass.

How It Works

Our processing chain has four steps:

  1. Read only what’s needed: For L-band, we read only the parts of NASA’s files that fall inside each site: 233 GB out of 11.9 TB of whole files. S-band files are downloaded whole and cropped to the sites: we downloaded 2.25 TB, and filtered it to the 23 GB we needed. Everything goes onto one shared grid.
  2. Measure change with standard radar statistics: We use a Quegan-Yu multi-temporal speckle filter, a likelihood-ratio test that dates each change, and log-ratio and coherence change maps. Interferometry measures ground motion, and pixel-offset tracking measures ice velocity.
  3. Name the change: Physics rules come first, then direct comparisons with reference maps, then machine learning where a single radar measurement isn’t enough to draw conclusions. Six gradient-boosted tree models (five LightGBM, one scikit-learn histogram boosting) turn radar signals into named changes: change type, burn scars from wildfires, open water from floods, crop type from each field’s growing season, clear-cuts from deforestation, and sea ice from ocean images. Each model is trained on NASA and partner reference data, then scored only on held-out sites the model wasn’t trained on.
  4. Test against independent data: Each site is checked against a non-NISAR reference, under a pass rule written down before scoring: NASA ITS_LIVE (glaciers), SMAP (soil moisture), Copernicus flood maps, official fire perimeters, national crop registers, and GNSS stations (earthquakes). Only sites that pass are published, but we also acknowledge the failures: 213 of 241 site records passed, and we held back 7 of those from publishing.

For example, at Thwaites Glacier, also called the “Doomsday Glacier,” Project Zeta maps ice speed at every point and finds that the fastest ice reaches 12.6 m/day. Against NASA’s ITS_LIVE, speeds agree within about 6% and flow directions within about 4 degrees. ISRO’s S-band passes the same test independently at this glacier, as well as at 8 other glacier sites that had S-band data, so the motion of each of those glaciers is measured twice.

Exploring the Website

Each of the 206 sites has its own page, which opens as a guided story: as the visitor scrolls through the numbered steps, the map beside the text changes from what the radar sees, to what changed and where, to the measured numbers, and finally to how the result compares with an independent reference. In Explore mode, the visitor takes over the map and can turn on any of the site’s layers; each layer is labeled as validated, experimental, not tested, or observation. We also include a short explanation of each layer, so that visitors can understand what they see, whether they are scientists, students, or curious citizens. A timeline lets them pick two dates or play a time-lapse through every NISAR pass, and clicking any pixel opens its full radar history, drawn against the curve its normal seasons would predict. Every layer can be downloaded from the website in GeoTIFF, CSV, or JSON format, and every map links back to the NASA files it came from.

The Compare tab places any two maps of the same site on top of each other, with a line the visitor can drag to sweep between them. Two dates of one layer show change, such as a river before and after a flood. Two layers of the same date show what each measurement responds to, such as HH against HV polarization or radar against optical satellite images. At the 58 sites that both radars imaged, visitors can also sweep between NASA’s L-band and ISRO’s S-band from the same pass. Every choice comes with an explanation of what it is, how to read it, and what the sweep between the two should reveal.

The Anywhere tab reaches beyond our sites to any point on Earth. A visitor can give coordinates, a place name, a click on the world map, or their own location. Project Zeta asks NASA’s archive, in real time, for every NISAR L-band product over that point. The report lists every date NISAR imaged that point and shows whether it returned every 12 days or skipped passes, along with the direction the radar was looking from and the imaging mode it used. It also says which of our 12 processes the data could support, and links to our nearest site for a full worked example. A time-lapse of NASA’s daily NISAR images plays beside an optical view of the same day.

Benefits

Project Zeta offers four main benefits:

  • Accessibility: Radar data usually needs massive storage, specialist software, and expert knowledge. Project Zeta provides plain-language maps with numbers, in both light and dark themes, in any modern web browser at any screen size.
  • Trust: Every published site passed an independent test. Our experimental layers are clearly labeled as experimental, and our limitations are stated openly.
  • Cost: Mirroring NISAR’s raw archive on cloud storage would cost over $100,000 a month. Project Zeta’s layers, even if extended to all of NISAR’s land, would cost only about $150 a month to host, because we read only what we need and publish the results, never copies of NISAR’s files.
  • Reproducibility: The whole radar record behind our sites fits on one ordinary disk, and anyone with a free NASA Earthdata account can check our numbers.

Intended Impact

Our intended impact is to make NISAR useful to people who will never open a radar file. Because radar works through cloud, smoke, and darkness, all the maps below can arrive every 12 days:

  • Emergency managers and fire agencies: Project Zeta maps the full extent of a burn within one NISAR cycle of the fire, without waiting for crews to walk the perimeter. Those maps show where slopes have lost their cover, which guides erosion warnings and replanting. Against official fire perimeters, 91% of what our model maps as burned is burned.
  • Flood responders and wetland managers: Project Zeta maps open flood water on every pass and follows its rise and fall through a whole season, so responders can see which areas stay under water longest. Several of our sites are on Asia’s floodplains, where most of the people exposed to river and monsoon floods live. Against Copernicus flood maps, our model finds 83% of the flood water.
  • Farmers and agricultural agencies: Project Zeta names the crop growing in each field from how its radar signal changes through the season, and dates each harvest to a 12-day window. Agencies can use this to forecast harvests and check subsidy claims without visiting every field. Against farmers’ own crop declarations, our model names the right crop in 82% of fields.
  • Drought and water managers: Project Zeta shows NISAR’s soil moisture at 200 m detail, where earlier satellites such as SMAP see only 9 km cells. That detail is fine enough to tell one farm or pasture from the next, providing an early signal of both drought and flood risk. Against NASA’s SMAP satellite, the soil wetting and drying we map matches with a median correlation of 0.73.
  • Forest monitors: Project Zeta finds new clearings of 5 hectares or more and dates each one to a 12-day window, in both boreal forests and the tropics. A dated alert can help agencies tell legal harvests from illegal clearing while the evidence is still fresh. Against official felling records, our model finds 85% of recorded clear-cuts.
  • Carbon and conservation planners: NISAR’s long L-band wave passes through leaves and responds to the wood in trunks and branches, so Project Zeta maps how much forest stands, not only where it is. Many of these sites are African woodlands, where field surveys are rare and carbon estimates are most uncertain. Against ESA’s biomass map, our radar measurement ranks forests by their wood with a median correlation of about 0.79.
  • City and regional planners: Project Zeta maps where buildings stand in 54 cities and regions, all measured the same way. Fast-growing cities often outrun their own maps, and a consistent footprint helps plan roads, services, and flood protection. Against the European Commission’s optical built-up map of the world, a built-up area is brighter in our radar maps than an open area 98% of the time.
  • Groundwater and infrastructure managers: Where too much groundwater is pumped, the land sinks: roads, pipes, and buildings can crack. Project Zeta measures that sinking to the centimeter across whole plains, showing which places sink fastest and where pumping limits would matter most. Against independent Sentinel-1 measurements, our sinking maps match with correlations of 0.72 to 0.96.
  • Earthquake and volcano scientists and responders: Ground instruments record an earthquake at a few points, while Project Zeta can map how far the ground moved across the whole region. At volcanoes, it outlines fresh lava and measures the swelling of the ground. Against GNSS ground stations, 89% of stations agree with the earthquake motion we measured.
  • Coastal communities and sea-level planners: Glaciers like Thwaites are among the largest uncertainties in how fast seas will rise. Project Zeta measures the flow of 9 of our 10 glaciers with both L-band and S-band, so an error in one would show up as a disagreement with the other. Against NASA’s ITS_LIVE, our ice speeds agree within 15% and flow directions within about 8 degrees at all 10 glaciers.
  • Arctic communities and shipping: Project Zeta marks where the ice edge lies in 16 polar seas on every pass. Knowing where ice ends and open water begins matters for safe travel, hunting, and shipping routes. Against the University of Bremen’s daily ice maps, our model correctly identifies 86% of the sea ice.
  • Students, teachers, and the public: Every site opens as a guided story in plain language, and we also include a glossary, tours, and links to NASA’s own trainings. Visitors can sweep between two radar images, hear a pixel’s history as sound, or look up their own hometown in the Anywhere tab.

For any scientist, Project Zeta offers an early, independent check of NISAR’s provisional data, along with some of the first public side-by-side tests of L-band and S-band.

Tools, Languages, Hardware, and Software

We developed Project Zeta with the following tools:

  • Hardware: All of our own processing, training, and building ran on a single laptop: our Apple MacBook Pro with the M3 Max chip and 128 GB of memory, supported by several external solid-state drives for a total of 16 TB of fast storage. Reading only the needed pieces of NISAR’s files is what made petabyte-scale data workable on one machine.
  • Data processing: Python with NumPy, SciPy, pandas, xarray, Dask, h5py, GDAL, rasterio, rio-cogeo, pyproj, Shapely, GeoPandas, Matplotlib, asf_search, and earthaccess.
  • Machine learning: LightGBM and scikit-learn, also in Python.
  • Website: TypeScript with React, Vite, and MapLibre GL; basemaps from Protomaps and OpenStreetMap; and hosting on Cloudflare Pages with R2.
  • Testing: Playwright in Chrome, Safari, Firefox, and Edge, at phone, tablet, laptop, and desktop sizes.
  • Data sources: NASA’s ASF DAAC, ISRO’s Bhoonidhi portal, NASA GIBS, OPERA, HLS, SMAP, ITS_LIVE, and GEDI, along with ESA, Copernicus, and many other datasets credited below.

Creativity

Project Zeta is creative in the questions it asks, the methods it builds, and the way it tells the story:

  • Both radars, treated the same way: NASA’s L-band and ISRO’s S-band go through identical code; because both image the same ground at the same moment, any difference between them is physics, not time. We wrote down our predictions before reading the S-band data, and we report the one that was wrong: L-band, not S-band, followed crop greening more closely.
  • A fair contest between wavelengths: Adding a second radar also adds more images, so we gave L-band the same number of extra images as a control. Three L-band and three S-band dates beat six L-band dates at 35 of 43 sites: the gain comes from the second wavelength itself.
  • New S-band methods: We rebuilt the viewing geometry from each S-band file’s own grids, after finding its direction tables pointed 55 to 100 degrees off. We wrote our own tracking for Thwaites’ fast ice, which outruns ISRO’s S-band offset product, and set a flood-water threshold inside each S-band image. To our knowledge, we also ran the first public test of S-band for measuring ground movement.
  • A borrowed calendar: NISAR’s record is too short to know a pixel’s normal year, so we learn its seasonal rhythm from years of Sentinel-1 images. That way, an ordinary seasonal swing is not mistaken for an event.
  • References built when none existed: We drew our own lava outlines from Sentinel-2 infrared images, and formed our own interferograms where NASA had none spanning the Caracas earthquake. At a Texas marsh, a NOAA tide gauge is the judge: the marsh must darken as the water rises, while nearby higher ground must not.
  • Beating the easy answer: Sea ice changes slowly, so each of our ice maps must do at least as well as reusing the reference map from 12 days earlier. Our clear-cut model learns from its own confirmed false alarms, and skips frozen dates, because frost changes a forest’s radar signal as much as felling does.
  • A full year over Houston: NASA released images from NISAR’s calibration months over only a few places, and Houston is one of them, giving us much more data for our own city. We used it to build a 353-day record, the longest on the website. We also present it alongside NASA’s airborne radar images of Hurricane Harvey for context.
  • Science for more than the eyes: Sonification plays any pixel’s radar history as music, one note for each NISAR pass, where a higher note means a brighter radar return. A flood or a harvest can then be heard as a sudden fall or rise in the melody, and an audible tick marks each change we detected. The scale is the same at every site, so a note means the same brightness in Africa as it does in Antarctica.
  • The mission’s promise beside its first evidence: Before launch, NASA described in white papers and interactive stories what NISAR was built to do for each kind of change. Each of our sites links to those pages, to NASA’s trainings in English and Spanish, and to the same area and dates in NASA’s own data tools. Visitors can read what NASA hoped the mission would show, then see what our early data and analyses show.

Factors We Considered

Our team considered how far each result can be trusted, who needs to be able to use it, and what it takes to keep it open to everyone:

  • A young mission: NISAR’s files are still marked provisional, so we could not assume every image was sound. We drop any date that covers less than half of a site or reads far darker than the rest, and we screen crop regions for radio interference. Each of our checks is therefore also an outside test of the new data itself.
  • A short record: Most sites have about four months of images, which is enough to catch an event but not a trend. For each process, we state what that record can and cannot support: a city’s footprint but not its growth, one flood season but not what is normal.
  • References that are not ground truth: Many of our references are themselves satellite estimates, and even two respected flood products from the same radar agree with each other on less than half of the water. Where a reference has that weakness, we call a pass “agreement”; where it is partly made from radar, we add a second independent check.
  • Chance: A statistical test run over millions of pixels and many dates will flag some by chance alone. No result on the website rests on one test: a named change must be supported by at least one of three independent kinds of evidence, and our training labels by two.
  • What radar cannot see: Water hidden under crops or trees does not look like open water to L-band, and steep slopes facing the radar are distorted. We flag those slopes, and we do not present floodplains as flood sites where the radar could not see the water. S-band covers only 58 of our sites, so we say where nothing can be said.
  • Choosing sites fairly: A website of hand-picked successes would prove little. For several processes, we chose the sites from the reference data alone, before looking at any radar image, and we publish the count of sites that failed beside those that passed. We also spread the sites across 7 continents and many countries.
  • Visitors of every ability: The website works by keyboard as well as by mouse, labels its controls for screen readers, offers its charts as tables, and respects a visitor’s reduced-motion setting. It adapts from a phone to a large desktop monitor, so no one needs special equipment to use it.
  • Credit where it is due: Project Zeta rests on the work of two space agencies and dozens of data providers. Every dataset is cited with its license and the credit line its provider asks for, and the website states that it is not an official NASA product. Our own maps, layers, and text are shared under CC BY 4.0, so others can reuse them with attribution.
  • Room to grow: NISAR adds new images every day, so the design had to stay affordable as it expands. Each new site needs only about 1.1 GB of L-band data, and the website runs without a server of our own to maintain.
